title: Strength Starts Before the Weight Room: What Counts for Kids and Teens
subtitle: For young people, getting stronger can begin with climbing, carrying and active play. If training becomes more structured, the essentials are good coaching, sound technique and a pace that fits the person—not the calendar.
imageAlt: Two adults encourage a child trying a climbing structure in a neighborhood playground, with space for other children to play nearby.

body: Start with a wider definition of strength

When a child or teenager asks about getting stronger, it is tempting to jump straight to weights, sets and a gym membership. But strength-building is broader than lifting equipment. Climbing a playground structure, doing push-ups, jumping, running and carrying everyday items all ask muscles to work against resistance or the body’s weight. These activities can be part of an active life without turning movement into a formal training program.

That broader view also helps families avoid treating a young person as a smaller adult. The useful first questions are less about how much they can lift and more about what movement they enjoy, what feels appropriate for their age and experience, and whether they have the support to learn safely. Strength is a capacity to build, not a test a child has to pass.
The weekly target is a guide, not a weight-room prescription

For children and adolescents ages 6–17, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance recommends at least 60 minutes of physical activity each day. It also calls for muscle- and bone-strengthening activity on at least three days a week. The examples include climbing and push-ups for muscles, and jumping and running for bones; the guidance is not asking every child to complete three gym sessions [1].

Think of the target as a way to notice whether a week includes varied movement. A child might climb, play tag, take part in a sport, dance, or choose a bodyweight activity. The point is not to add up every minute with a stopwatch or make a family’s schedule feel like a training plan. It is to make room for regular activity that is accessible and enjoyable, while recognizing that circumstances, ability and interests differ.
Play can be the right starting point

For younger children, active play often offers a natural setting to practise pushing, pulling, jumping, balancing and climbing. These movements develop coordination and physical confidence as well as strength. A family can make space for them by visiting a playground, walking to a park, or choosing an active game that fits the child’s interests and the available environment. No equipment purchase is required for movement to count.

CDC guidance notes that younger children generally do not need formal weightlifting programs, while adolescents may take part in structured programs [1]. That distinction is not a deadline or a judgment about who is “ready.” It leaves room for differences in development, experience and preference. A child who is not interested in organized training can still build strength through active play. A teenager who is curious about resistance training can explore it with appropriate instruction rather than being left to guess from videos or comparisons with peers.
A structured program should teach before it tests

Resistance training includes more than barbells and machines: it can involve bodyweight exercises and other forms of resistance. The American Academy of Pediatrics emphasizes qualified supervision, sound technique and progression suited to a young person’s development. The goal of a well-designed program is to teach movement and build capacity in a controlled way—not to see how much a child can lift in a single effort [2].

Before enrolling, ask who will supervise, what experience they have working with children and adolescents, and how they teach and adapt movements. Ask how the coach responds when a participant is tired, uncomfortable or unsure, and how progress is adjusted as skills improve. A good answer should make room for questions and individual differences. If the program’s appeal rests mainly on heavy lifts, competition or rapid physical change, families can look for a setting that puts learning and safety first.
Make the first steps small and observable

If a young person wants to try structured training, begin with a conversation about what they hope to do: feel more capable, learn a skill, support a sport or simply explore a new activity. Then look for a qualified adult who can show a movement, watch the young person practise it and offer corrections that are specific and understandable. A starting session should leave room to learn, rather than becoming a test of strength.

Families can help by agreeing on a few practical expectations: follow the coach’s instructions, use equipment only as taught, and say when something hurts or feels wrong. The coach should be able to explain how the program progresses and how it changes when a young person is still learning. There is no need to copy an adult routine or race another participant’s progress. Build skill first; allow added challenge to follow only when the supervisor judges it appropriate.

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis examined 22 studies of supervised strength training in children and adolescents ages 6–16. Its authors reported improvements in measured fitness outcomes across the included programs [3]. That is encouraging evidence for supervised youth training, but it is not a ready-made routine for every child. The programs varied, and the review noted that they did not stratify results by biological maturity. A finding across studies should not be mistaken for a prescription for one person.

The AAP report says well-designed resistance-training programs have not been shown to harm growth-plate health or linear growth [2]. That reassurance applies to programs designed and supervised appropriately; it should not be stretched to cover unsupervised maximal lifting or any activity done through pain. Research and guidance support thoughtful participation, not a promise that every program, coach or exercise is suitable for every young person.
Health, access and the young person’s own goals

Some young people may have a health condition or other circumstance that changes how they should approach a training program. The AAP advises families to consult a medical professional before starting when specified health conditions are present [2]. If a caregiver is uncertain, asking the young person’s health professional about the activity and any needed adaptations is a sensible first step. That conversation can support participation rather than automatically rule it out.

Access matters, too. A good starting point might be a school or community program, an accessible playground, an adaptive activity group, or movement at home. Ask what adaptations are available, whether a coach can explain exercises in more than one way, and whether the young person can take breaks or modify a movement. Include the child or teen in these choices. Their comfort, interests and sense of agency belong in the plan—not just an adult’s ambitions for their performance.
A family check before signing up

Before committing to a program, take a few minutes to ask the young person what they want from it and what would help them feel comfortable. Together, check three things: Is there a supervisor qualified to work with their age group? Does the program teach technique and adjust challenge to the participant? Can the young person ask questions, stop when something feels wrong and take part without being pressured to lift more than they are ready for?

If the answers are clear and reassuring, consider trying a session and reviewing how it felt afterward—not by grading performance, but by asking what they learned, what they enjoyed and what they would change. If the fit is poor, another setting or a return to active play is a valid next move. The aim is not to move every child into a weight room. It is to help young people find safe, worthwhile ways to use their bodies and build confidence over time.
